On the same tasks, agents in low-resource languages also consume substantially more tokens than in English (up to roughly twice the input) without proportional increases in interaction length, and language consistency degrades further on tasks requiring structured output, where switches are directed overwhelmingly toward English. We believe BabelArena provides a foundation for advancing research on reliable and efficient multilingual agents.

articles.title: Framing the Narrative: Ideological Mimicry in Large Language Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.38256v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer questions about politically contentious issues, yet evaluations typically treat a model's stance as a relatively stable property. Real users, however, communicate political signals through their terminology, assumptions, and personal context. We investigate whether such signals produce ideological mimicry: systematic shifts in the political stance expressed by an LLM toward the position conveyed by the interaction. If LLMs adapt their responses to these signals, they risk creating personalised political information environments in which users with opposing views receive systematically different accounts of the same issue, potentially reinforcing existing divisions. We build the Poli-SHIFT dataset and evaluation framework and assess ten LLMs across ten contentious political topics in the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia, systematically manipulating contested terminology, politically valenced premises, and user information, and eliciting responses in both multiple-choice and open-text formats. Across models, we find robust evidence that prompt framing shapes the political stance of LLM outputs. Substituting contested terminology while holding the substantive question fixed reverses which side of an issue a model supports in 16.9% of matched item pairs for open-weight models and 4.2% for closed-source models. Stated political ideology also systematically shifts responses toward the user's position. These findings show that political stance is not a fixed property of LLMs; the views expressed are conditional on the interaction with the user. As LLMs become increasingly personalised sources of information, such interaction-dependent adaptation could contribute to political information environments that reinforce users' existing perspectives.

articles.title: ContextAdapt: Evaluating Contextual Adaptation and Value Alignment in LLMs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.38260v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Values such as honesty, autonomy, and confidentiality are often regarded as general principles underpinning AI alignment. However, what it means to act in accordance with these values can depend on the context in which a decision is made. In this paper, we ask whether large language models (LLMs) appropriately adapt the application of a value across professional settings, while remaining consistent when contextual changes do not alter the relevant professional norm. To study this, we introduce ContextAdapt, an evaluation framework covering honesty, autonomy, and confidentiality across medicine, law, finance, and national security. Drawing on primary-source professional and regulatory documents, we construct a value x domain framework and use this to develop scenarios testing both default professional rules and recognised exceptions. We evaluate 12 LLMs on both the actions they recommend and the justifications they provide. In our main experiment, models achieve 95.9% mean action-level appropriateness, although the use of the correct domain-specific justification varies substantially across models, from 25.6% to 76.9%. In a separate factorial experiment, explicitly naming the professional domain and changing the role of the model have limited effect on behaviour, whereas changing stakes produces a 10.3-point average difference between low- and high-stakes conditions and severe but localised failures. These results show that evaluating value alignment requires us to consider not only whether models follow abstract principles, but whether they apply them appropriately across different contexts.

articles.title: Exploring the Hidden Cost of the World Around AI Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2609.38469v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Agent benchmarks test what agents can do in environments that are built for their tasks. Deployed agents work in the real world where other people and tools can change the state. An agent booking a flight may receive a message from someone else to change the destination, or a booking tool may fail without saying whether the ticket was purchased. We present BACKDROP, which asks how much of an agent's capability in a clean world survives in a non-cooperative world. BACKDROP takes a task along with the agent's execution environment, and plants four everyday hazards in its environment, one at a time and all together. Each hazard tests a different behavior. Authority: does a non-author actor instruction, from anyone who did not author the task, override the user's goal? Injection: does text planted in a record redirect the agent? Boundary: does the agent make changes in an app the user's task did not require? Fault: after a write fails without saying whether it landed, does the agent check before it retries? Across 3,678 variants and 16 models, the average pass rate falls from 69.5% to 31.3% once all four hazards are present; the strongest models fall furthest (Claude Fable 5.1 from 96.6% to 56.0%). The gap is consistent throughout all 16 models. BACKDROP formalizes these gaps and shows how an agent's score in a task's world is a ceiling on real-world performance.

articles.title: TrustMI: Causally controlling how assistants trust their users
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.06064v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) assistants routinely decide whether they can trust users and third parties whose competence, intentions, and integrity they cannot verify. This uncertainty matters for safety, as trusting the wrong party can lead an agent to comply with harmful requests or act on malicious instructions encountered during tool use. To study this problem, we define trust as an assistant's willingness to accept vulnerability to the actions of another party and ask whether such behavior can be causally controlled through model activations. We build 2,000 contrastive conversations spanning ability, benevolence, and integrity, where paired responses complete the same request but differ in whether the assistant trusts the user. From these pairs, we learn steering matrices while keeping the model parameters frozen and test them across six instruction-tuned models from three families, finding that steering changes trust decisions monotonically in both directions. We then ask whether this effect extends to several safety-related agent settings involving harmful requests, prompt injections, and insider threats, while using benign-task and reasoning as controls. Our findings provide evidence that trust in the user can be causally controlled along linear directions in model activations and provide a way to study how trust shapes safety-relevant behavior in language models.

articles.title: The interpreter as developer: An autoethnographic design study of building a computer-assisted interpreting tool through human-LLM co-creation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.16460v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Computer-assisted interpreting (CAI) tools are built for interpreters, mainly by third parties, and the interpreters' own side of development has received little first-person documentation. This article reports an autoethnographic design study in which a professional conference interpreter without formal programming training built a local-first CAI system through expert-led human-LLM co-creation. Analysis of the development dialogues shows how tacit professional knowledge became design only after generic defaults had failed in use, a reversal of the usual direction of technological mediation, from adopting tools to authoring them. Three mechanisms of in-booth appropriation emerged under a human-led division of labor, and a four-layer reconstruction illustrates the human contribution at work. First-month telemetry, over six thousand utterances across nine sessions, shows a fully local system sustaining translation-stage latencies near one second, with sustained-load degradation as a working boundary. The case bears on professional agency, knowledge production, and the training of interpreters under generative AI.

articles.title: Diagnosing and Mitigating Long-Session Degradation in Full-Duplex Speech Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.34991v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: End-to-end full-duplex spoken dialogue models enable natural, real-time spoken interactions with interruptions, backchannels, and overlapping speech. Prior evaluations have assessed diverse interaction capabilities and identified some degradation patterns across conversational turns. However, how model behavior evolves over extended sessions remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we address this gap by systematically characterizing long-session degradation and developing efficient methods to mitigate it. We introduce a closed-loop evaluation framework for long-session stability and apply it to several publicly available full-duplex speech models, revealing degradation over time in responsiveness, spoken content quality, and voice consistency. To mitigate this degradation, we propose a self-distillation-based training framework for lightweight LoRA adaptation that improves long-session stability with a small amount of additional training. We further introduce a two-resolution context (TRC) architecture that preserves recent interactions in full detail while compressing older interaction history into key-value representations. We evaluate our methods on three models with distinct architectures, assessing long-session stability, information retention, and computational efficiency. Across all three models, we show that LoRA adaptation mitigates performance degradation over ten-minute sessions, while adding TRC extends these gains beyond the training session length and reduces KV-cache growth by more than 90%.

articles.title: GEPA-Curator: Curated Learning for Self Improving Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.37651v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in multi-turn agentic workloads that require sustained interaction with complex environments. Existing reflective prompt optimizers such as GEPA learn from failed rollouts, but agentic failures can also come from prompt weaknesses, harness limitations, stochastic execution, or noisy judges. We argue that such failures may not provide useful learning signal, and may even be harmful; and thus it is essential to curate which tasks are provided to the prompt optimizer for better performance. We introduce GEPA-Curator, a framework that augments the prompt optimizer to select which agent experiences should shape prompt optimization. In particular, GEPA-Curator consists of two components: task curation, which filters out tasks that are likely to provide noisy or unreliable learning signals, and prior success retrieval, which selectively retrieves past successful trajectories for a task and provides them as additional context to the prompt optimizer. We evaluate GEPA-Curator on GoBrowse, ALFWorld, AppWorld, and $\tau$-bench, using both Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 5 as optimizer models. GEPA-Curator matches or exceeds the mean performance of both baselines, with gains of up to 20.7% over GEPA and 21.2% over ACE.

articles.title: The FlightFinder Occurrence Corpus: harmonising 128 aviation-safety source codes into one deduplicated cross-national accident dataset
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.37671v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: National aviation-investigation databases are deep but territorial; global compilations such as the Aviation Safety Network and the Bureau of Aircraft Accidents Archives are hand-curated, apply their own inclusion thresholds, and publish no field-level lineage. The FlightFinder Occurrence Corpus harmonizes 279,485 occurrences and 131,882 attached narratives from 128 source codes - national accident-investigation authorities, occurrence-reporting systems and four global compilations. Records are mapped into one schema; apart from a duplicate pre-filter on three sources, each normalized record reduces to exactly one key from an ordered ladder - event signature, registration and date, rounded position and date, or source and native identifier - so a missing field never creates a link, and the key is the occurrence identifier. Records the ladder cannot reach are scored in a blocked pass into an explicit merge table and applied only within an automatically approved score band or after a person confirms them. Field conflicts follow a documented source ranking; one provenance row per contributing source - its record identifier and URL - is retained, with attribution and licence terms per source code. Linkage error is measured on five adjudicated samples totalling 200 pairs. A recorded uniform random draw of 60 from the 3,441 merges the automatic band applies as it ships found no error; the exact two-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson upper bound on its false-merge rate is 6.0%, or 205 pairs. The measured error covers the scored band only; the ladder's deterministic joins are not adjudicated. The corpus has no exposure denominators and inherits the under-reporting of its sources. It is offered as a base for cross-national safety statistics, source-disagreement studies and narrative text mining; a frozen, DOI-referenced snapshot accompanies the live API.

articles.title: Write Facts the Way Models Read Them: Lifting the Two-Hop Curse
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.01519v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A language model that learns a new fact by fine-tuning can repeat it but cannot reason with it: taught that a person is a citizen of a new country, it still cannot say, without chain-of-thought, who the head of state of that person's country is. This two-hop curse is widely treated as a reasoning deficit, and the strongest knowledge editors answer it with synthesized reasoning data. We show that the reasoning is intact and the writing is wrong. Fine-tuning writes a new fact as an answer to be said, whereas the second hop reads the bridge ("that person's country") as an entity, from the middle layers on: patching the model's own representation of the entity into the bridge at those layers largely restores the second hop, yet after fine-tuning the bridge there is no closer to the new entity than before the edit. We therefore propose read-equivalent writing (Legible): one loss term makes the bridge phrase, at the layer where the second hop finishes reading it, match the model's own reading of the new entity, and keeps the same relation's other subjects unchanged. Phrases and targets come from the edited model itself, and no multi-hop training data is used. Across Qwen2.5, Llama-3 and Qwen3, Legible (I) composes learned facts more often than the model composes its own knowledge, on MQuAKE's two-hop-curse questions; (II) reaches 1.8-2.6x the bridge accuracy of CaKE, whose reasoning data composes no better than plain fine-tuning, and has the best average over composition, accuracy and locality against four families of writers; and (III) lifts the curse on RippleEdits, on the benchmark of Balesni et al., who named the curse, and at 14B.

articles.title: Visual Similarity in Adult Word Extension and Artificial Word Learning
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.14116v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: When two objects share a name, how much does their visual similarity explain, and what do the teaching examples add? We studied word extension across ten visual representations: eight trained encoders, a randomly initialized network, and raw pixels. Reanalyzing trial-level data from a large adult word-extension study (Lewis & Frank, 2018; 520 people), we computed each test image's distance to the teaching examples. Within the taught domain, greater distance was associated with less extension for all eight trained encoders and for the untrained network, so the association cannot be attributed only to what the encoders learned; raw pixels showed no negative association. In post hoc models that let the distance slope vary across images, seven of the eight trained encoders retained a negative estimate and five had 95% intervals entirely below zero; the interval of the reference encoder included zero. Whether trial order changes the distance slope, the frozen primary question, remained inconclusive. Example composition changed extension at comparable distances: after three examples, adults extended a word to 1.1% of superordinate items when the examples were subordinate and to 77.5% when they were superordinate. In artificial learners, words joining more distant categories were learned less accurately for six of the eight trained encoders. Every trained encoder correlated with human similarity measures from three datasets, and so did the untrained network, although far more weakly than the trained encoders other than MAE on two of them. In an exploratory comparison on the same images, no common threshold on any trained encoder reproduced the adults' narrow-to-broad gain (at most 66.67 vs. 76.43 percentage points). Cosine distance to the centroid of the teaching examples predicts part of word extension, but does not capture the effect of example composition.

articles.title: Offline-First Quantized AI: Design and Evaluation of an On-Device Maternal-Health Assistant for Low-Connectivity Environments
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.20012v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Offline language models could extend access to maternal-health information where internet connectivity is unreliable, but deployment requires both clinically appropriate responses and feasible local execution. This study evaluated an Android assistant using ready-made quantized models, a clinically validated local knowledge package, conversation history, and optional local retrieval. Gemma 4 E2B and Qwen3.5 0.8B were compared on 45 conversations and 312 turns per configuration. Gemma retained context more consistently, whereas Qwen generated faster and used less memory. Clinician assessment of 150 Gemma responses across nine clinical domains yielded a mean quality score of 3.80/4, with 147 responses meeting the acceptance criterion. In 74 matched RAG-on/off questions, 11 RAG-on answers improved, 52 were comparable, four were degraded by returned content, and seven were lower-rated without clear evidence that retrieval caused the difference. Full-cohort mean differences were small and uncertain. In a sensitivity analysis excluding flagged cases, RAG-on had descriptively higher mean usefulness, safety, correctness, and actionability in the conditional 70-pair subset excluding the four flagged pairs from both conditions. Physical- device testing demonstrated offline responses on a 6 GB Android handset, with a 14.3 s median latency, alongside successful reconnection synchronization in the integrated application. Together, the findings characterize the integrated offline maternal-health assistant within the designed and tested benchmark, retrieval pipeline, and handset conditions.

articles.title: When Should Decision Models Compare Candidates?
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.20335v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Language-model agents frequently select among candidate actions, such as tools and web elements. Should decision models score candidates independently or allow their scores to depend on other candidates? We investigate this question by comparing three approaches: Pointwise scoring, Setwise scoring, and Candidate Attention. Across five agent-decision benchmarks, Pointwise scoring remains competitive, while Setwise scoring performs better on some tool-selection and binary-decision tasks. Candidate Attention does not consistently improve upon Pointwise scoring, despite allowing cross-candidate interaction. Using two controlled synthetic tasks, we further examine whether models learn to use candidate-set information. With targeted relational training, Setwise models learn candidate dependencies and generalize to shifted inputs, while Candidate Attention shows weaker transfer. Our results show that access to other candidates does not guarantee effective comparison, and that its benefits depend on both task requirements and training.

articles.title: Silent Arbitration: How Large Language Models Resolve Co-Authoritative Conflicting Instructions
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.27444v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models increasingly receive high-level instructions about roles, values, interests, and communication style. Such instructions can conflict even when a prompt assigns them equal authority and provides no priority rule. We study co-authoritative persona conflict, in which a single prompt jointly assigns two opposing personas. Across eight conflict types grounded in published source material and five LLMs, we measure conflict acknowledgment, resolution strategy, and directional stance. Models acknowledge incompatibility in 72% of direct checks but explicitly surface it in only 22% of task responses, revealing silent arbitration. Dominance accounts for 45% of dual-persona responses, and 35% of compromise-labeled responses retain directional lean. Prompt framing further changes the visible form of arbitration substantially more than ordinary paraphrase variation. These findings show that evaluating instruction following should assess whether models disclose conflicts, how they resolve them, and which persona their responses favor.

articles.title: Grammar-as-a-Drafter: More Tokens per Speculative Decoding Step on Grammar-Constrained Structured Outputs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.28349v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up generation by letting a lightweight drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in one forward pass. Under structured outputs (JSON schemas, regular expressions, tool-call formats), the drafter works against a constraint it does not know, so its proposals for keys, delimiters, and indentation are often rejected or invalid, even though the grammar engine already knows the next tokens.
  We present Grammar-as-a-Drafter (GaaD), which makes the grammar a second drafter. Before each verify step, the scheduler merges the drafter's proposal with grammar-forced tokens (out-degree 1 in the grammar automaton) into one draft row of width $K$ (which can exceed the drafter's proposal length $K_M$): matching tokens are promoted to GRAMMAR, the proposal is truncated where it disagrees, and grammar tokens fill the remaining slots. The verify step accepts GRAMMAR drafts without computing their logits, composing with any drafter without adding kernels or compilation on the critical path. Because grammars fix text rather than tokens, accepting canonical GRAMMAR drafts with probability 1 preserves grammar validity but can shift the output distribution relative to grammar-masked decoding.
  We implement GaaD in vllm-torchtpu and an independent Rust serving runtime, and evaluate it on TPU v7x with MTP, DFlash, and n-gram drafters on a JSON character-profile benchmark. GaaD raises average acceptance length from 2.06 to 5.43 for MTP (Qwen3.5-0.8B; 1.99 to 5.31 on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), 1.57 to 4.13 for DFlash, and 1.30 to 3.64 for n-gram (Qwen3-4B), decoding 2.66-2.81x faster at batch size 1 and 1.14-1.70x faster at batch size 64. In the Rust runtime, MTP with GaaD is 2.23x faster on Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2.02x on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 (1.22-1.69x at high concurrency). Under mixed traffic, GaaD finishes workloads 1.03-1.23x sooner while modestly raising plain-text TPOT.

articles.title: LITMUS - Literature Informed Testbed for Mapping Usecases and Synthesizing Risk-Cards
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.29034v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in real-world applications has heightened the need for systematic, safety-oriented deployment frameworks. Existing approaches typically prioritize the construction of datasets and risk cards around the LLM and AI architecture itself, yet they provide scant consideration for the specific use-case that drives model selection. This omission is problematic because any practical AI deployment begins with a detailed use-case description that informs the assessment of contextual hazards. In this paper, we introduce a structured pipeline that, given a use-case, automatically produces a tailored dataset and an accompanying risk card. The process ensures that identified risks are tightly coupled to the use-case, and it offers traceable evidence from peer-reviewed literature to substantiate each risk to use-case relationship. Prior claim-verification methods (FActScore, FactReasoner) have been validated for factual claims. Risk-relevance is a hypothetical claim about possible harm, and whether evidence retrieval can meaningfully assess such claims remains untested. Literature-Informed Testbed for Mapping Use-cases and Synthesizing (LITMUS) risk cards are the first systematic attempt to characterize this adaptation. We evaluated the pipeline using the MIT Risk Taxonomy and achieved a 0.91 F1-score with a list of 320 samples from the benchmark risk dataset that was considered. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in generating robust, evidence-based risk assessments for LLM deployments.

articles.title: S\'anchez, Feij\'oo, or Abascal? Speaker Attribution and Ideological Congruence in LLM Personas Reading Posts on X of the Leaders of the Three Main Parties of the 29N General Election in Spain
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.29765v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Source cues are central to political communication, yet reception studies with large language model (LLM) personas as synthetic audiences have not tested whether personas respond to who speaks and not only to what is said. With Spain's general election of 29 November 2026 in mind, we run a speaker-attribution experiment using 1,075 anonymised X posts by the leaders of PSOE, PP and VOX on four topics (the economy and employment, household costs, immigration and corruption) and 791 distinct value-grounded, LLM-generated personas. Each post was assigned to 300 topic-selected persona profiles, 150 grounded in the Inglehart-Welzel cultural map and 150 in Moral Foundations Theory, under four conditions: no author, S\'anchez, Feij\'oo or Abascal, yielding 322,470 complete persona-post quartets. Naming any leader lowered support for identical text, with the penalty for Abascal nearly twice as large as those for S\'anchez and Feij\'oo. The penalty follows the persona's elicited left-right self-placement (ideological congruence): left personas spare S\'anchez and right personas spare Feij\'oo, although ideology was never in the message-evaluation prompt. Corruption posts were penalised under every name, whereas on other topics the ideologically closest leader generally produced little or no penalty. The leader order matches public opinion in 48 CIS barometers (2022-2026) in all three groups and the sign of all twelve differences, but fits barometers before the model's 2024 knowledge cutoff better than recent ones. Our findings demonstrate that LLM personas evaluate political speakers through systematic, value-congruent priors: however, while they replicate human candidate rank-orders across survey barometers, this alignment is ordinal rather than quantitative, highlighting their utility for controlled source-effect experiments though not as substitutes for empirical public opinion surveys.

articles.title: LimeTree: Linear-Memory Graph Neural Networks over Tree-Graphs for Resource-Efficient Language Modeling and Context Extrapolation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.30934v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The search for computationally efficient alternatives to the Transformer has yielded numerous architectures in recent years; however, most exhibit severe weaknesses in associative recall-such as key-value (KV) retrieval-and length extrapolation, where even standard Transformers struggle. This paper introduces LimeTree, a linear-complexity architecture in both memory and compute for sequence modeling. By integrating synthetic KV retrieval tasks directly into standard language modeling training, LimeTree achieves strong perplexity alongside reliable recall. Two variants were evaluated on WikiText-103 and PG-19 under strict compute constraints. On WikiText-103, LimeTree reaches a token-level perplexity of 19 in just 6 hours on four Quadro RTX 8000 GPUs, while maintaining 100\% KV retrieval accuracy even when extrapolating from a training context length of 512 to an evaluation length of 16,384. On PG-19, the model achieves a token-level perplexity of 10.84 in 35.5 hours on a single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU with minimal hyperparameter tuning. These results position LimeTree as a competitive linear-complexity alternative to Transformers, combining superior perplexity and training throughput with robust in-context retrieval and length extrapolation.

articles.title: Unlocking the Power of Loops in Pretrained LLMs with Loop Residuals
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.31094v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Looped Transformers iterate a shared block of layers to increase computation without adding parameters, offering stronger performance and test-time scaling. However, this power has so far required training from scratch and yielded only modest gains for LLMs. Finetuning existing models into loops is far cheaper, yet also brings only marginal gains over SFT. We propose LoopRes, an effective, scalable, and simple approach that turns loops into significant and consistent gains for pretrained LLMs. Building on Attention Residuals, LoopRes lets each looped layer attend directly to the outputs of earlier loops. Since these outputs are iterates of the same layers and become harder to tell apart, we give each a trainable loop-aware key that encodes its structural identity. Attending to all earlier loops also lets layers skip intermediate ones, so we restrict each layer to a residual window of the latest W loops, forcing every loop to build incrementally on recent ones. Across 6 pretrained LLMs from 3 model families and 9 benchmarks, LoopRes delivers significant and consistent gains: at 2x compute, it improves Qwen3-1.7B-Base by 29.1% over SFT, more than doubling the gain of the state-of-the-art baseline. The gains hold on larger models up to 30B and across all three families. More importantly, from 1.7B to 8B, LoopRes scales more steeply than SFT as compute grows, reaching a higher ceiling while needing less compute on long outputs. These results establish LoopRes as an effective looping approach, delivering both better performance and better test-time scaling.

articles.title: MMGenBench: An Automated Pipeline for Evaluating LMMs from a Text-to-Image Generation Perspective
articles.summary:
arXiv:2411.14062v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Existing benchmarks often rely on predefined questions or reference captions, limiting their flexibility for evaluating detailed descriptions on new image collections. We present MMGenBench, an automated benchmark framework for evaluating Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) from raw images without per-image questions or reference captions. The pipeline generates descriptions, reconstructs images with a frozen text-to-image model, and compares the original and reconstructed images using a frozen image encoder. It produces reusable per-image scores and inspectable reconstructions, supporting both model comparison and diagnosis of reconstructible visual information. We construct MMGenBench-Domain with 10,000 generated images and MMGenBench-Test with 1,284 images spanning 13 overlapping visual patterns. Evaluation of 68 LMMs reveals pattern-specific differences in reconstruction quality that overall scores can obscure. On 1,000 human-labeled caption pairs from six models, the default score achieves 90.00\% sample-level agreement. Factual perturbations and component analyses characterize the score's sensitivity under the evaluated pipeline, while a COCO study provides initial validation on natural photographs. MMGenBench complements existing benchmarks by linking automated comparisons to visual evidence of the information preserved in LMM descriptions. Project page: https://github.com/lerogo/MMGenBench.

articles.title: Where is the multimodal goal post? On the Ability of Foundation Models to Recognize Highlights in Videos
articles.summary:
arXiv:2601.16333v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Foundation models are used for many real-world applications involving language understanding and generation from temporally-ordered multimodal events. In this work, we study the ability of models to identify the most important sub-events in a video, which is a fundamental prerequisite for summarizing, reasoning over, or narrating multimodal events. Specifically, we focus on football games and evaluate models on their ability to distinguish between important and non-important sub-events in a game. To this end, we construct a new dataset by leveraging publicly available football highlight reels containing the most important moments of a game according to professional experts, without any additional annotation costs. Using our dataset, we compare several state-of-the-art multimodal models and show that they fail to reliably capture contextual importance. Analyses of models beyond standard evaluation metrics reveal their tendency to rely on a single dominant modality and their ineffectiveness in synthesizing necessary information from multiple sources. Our findings underline the importance of modular architectures that dynamically adapt to multimodal heterogeneity and the need for complementary training procedures that maximize cross-modal synergy.

articles.title: Diagnosing and Repairing Citation Failures in Generative Engine Optimization
articles.summary:
arXiv:2603.09296v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) aims to improve content visibility in AI-generated responses. However, existing methods measure contribution (how much a document influences a response) rather than citation, the mechanism that actually drives traffic back to creators. Also, these methods apply generic rewriting rules uniformly, failing to diagnose why individual documents are not cited. This paper introduces a diagnostic approach to GEO that asks why a document fails to be cited and intervenes accordingly. We develop a unified framework comprising: (1) the first taxonomy of citation failure modes spanning different stages of a citation pipeline; (2) AgentGEO, an agentic system that diagnoses failures using this taxonomy, selects targeted repairs from a corresponding tool library, and iterates until citation is achieved; and (3) a document-centric benchmark evaluating whether optimizations generalize across held-out queries. AgentGEO achieves 15-40% relative improvement in citation rates across engines and citation methods, while modifying only 5% of content, compared to 25% for baselines. Our analysis reveals that generic optimization can harm long-tail content and some documents face challenges that optimization alone cannot fully address, findings with implications for equitable visibility in AI-mediated information access.

articles.title: Speak or Stay Silent: Context-Aware Turn-Taking in Multi-Party Dialogue
articles.summary:
arXiv:2603.11409v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Existing voice AI assistants treat every detected pause as an invitation to speak. This works in dyadic dialogue, but in multi-party settings, where an AI assistant participates alongside multiple speakers, pauses are abundant and ambiguous. An assistant that speaks on every pause becomes disruptive rather than useful. In this work, we formulate context-aware turn-taking: at every detected pause, given the full conversation context, our method decides whether the assistant should speak or stay silent. We introduce a benchmark of over 120K labeled conversations spanning three multi-party corpora. Evaluating eight recent large language models, we find that they consistently fail at context-aware turn-taking under zero-shot prompting. We then propose a supervised fine-tuning approach with reasoning traces, improving balanced accuracy by up to 23 percentage points. Our findings suggest that context-aware turn-taking is not an emergent capability; it must be explicitly trained.

articles.title: The Reasoning Bottleneck in Graph-RAG: Structured Prompting and Context Compression for Multi-Hop QA
articles.summary:
arXiv:2603.14045v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Graph-RAG systems achieve strong multi-hop question answering by indexing documents into knowledge graphs, but strong retrieval does not guarantee strong answers. Evaluating KET-RAG, a leading Graph-RAG system, on three multi-hop QA benchmarks (HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA), we find that 77% to 91% of questions have the gold answer in the retrieved context, yet accuracy is only 35% to 78%, and 73% to 84% of errors are reasoning failures. We propose two augmentations: (i) SPARQL chain-of-thought prompting, which decomposes questions into triple-pattern queries aligned with the entity-relationship context, and (ii) graph-walk compression, which compresses the context by ~60% via knowledge-graph traversal with no LLM calls. SPARQL CoT improves accuracy by +2 to +14 pp; graph-walk compression adds +6 pp on average when paired with structured prompting on smaller models. Surprisingly, we show that, with question-type routing, a fully augmented budget open-weight Llama-8B model matches or exceeds the unaugmented Llama-70B baseline on all three benchmarks at ~12x lower cost. A replication on LightRAG confirms that our augmentations transfer across Graph-RAG systems.

articles.title: Pothen: Can Vision-Language Models Tell Where a Cultural Object Comes From?
articles.summary:
arXiv:2604.07338v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: A cultural object is a trace of the people who made it, and knowing who made it, where, and when shapes how it is catalogued, valued, and returned. Vision-language models now describe such objects for museum collections, yet whether they can recover this knowledge from an image has not been tested. We introduce Pothen, a benchmark of 750 objects from the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Getty in which a model predicts an object's title, culture, period, origin, and creator from its image alone, scored against curator-written catalogue records by an LLM judge calibrated on human annotation. Across nine models, mean field scores are 36.16% to 49.82%, but all five fields match for only 2.13% to 7.87% of objects. Images raise culture, period, and origin scores by 12.6 to 32.2 points for two models tested without them, and 83.52% of creator matches occur alongside an incorrect field. Models read visual evidence and hold facts about objects but do not bind them into one attribution, and in our error analysis their attributions follow the style an object resembles rather than the record of its making.

articles.title: PairAlign: A Framework for Autoregressive Tokenization via Self-Alignment with Applications to Audio Tokenization
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.06582v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Modern learning systems represent perceptual signals with continuous vectors, but comparison, retrieval, memory, alignment, and reasoning are often symbolic. In language, tokens provide this interface; for speech and audio, it must be learned. Existing audio tokenizers rely on local quantization, clustering, or reconstruction, leaving sequence consistency, compactness, length, termination, and edit geometry only indirectly controlled. We introduce PairAlign, a framework for compact audio tokenization through autoregressive self-alignment. An encoder maps speech to a continuous condition, and an autoregressive decoder emits tokens from BOS to EOS. Given two content-preserving views, PairAlign derives a canonical anchor target and trains both views to predict it, with unrelated in-batch targets as competing sequences. It first learns an autoregressive bridge from VQ targets and then transitions to EMA-teacher self-alignment with grounding and anti-collapse controls. On 3 s speech, PairAlign produces shorter, non-degenerate sequences while retaining ordered paired-view consistency. On the TIMIT retrieval archive, it operates at 8.28 tokens/s, reducing archive token count by 70.65% and the edit-distance work proxy by 91.87% relative to Stage I. Positive-negative probes show strong separation across phone-disjoint, trigram-disjoint, and temporally rearranged negatives, while rate-controlled post-hoc BPE does not recover the same compactness-consistency operating point. These results expose a rate-granularity trade-off: PairAlign does not uniformly outperform denser tokenizers on every local metric, but provides a lower-rate symbolic interface preserving ordered and relational structure. Conceptually, PairAlign follows JEPA-style predictive learning by predicting an abstract target rather than reconstructing the input; here, the target is a learned variable-length symbolic sequence.

articles.title: MobileMoE: Scaling On-Device Mixture of Experts
articles.summary:
arXiv:2605.27358v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has become the de facto architecture for hundred-billion-parameter language models, yet its advantages at sub-billion scales for on-device deployment remain largely unexplored. To close this gap, we present MobileMoE, a family of on-device MoE language models with sub-billion active parameters (0.3-0.9B active and 1.3-5.3B total) that establish a new Pareto frontier for on-device LLMs. We first formulate an on-device MoE scaling law that jointly optimizes MoE architecture under mobile memory and compute constraints, identifying an on-device sweet spot - moderate sparsity with fine-grained and shared experts - that is simultaneously memory and compute-optimal. Building on the derived architectures, we train MobileMoE with a four-stage recipe covering pre-training, mid-training, instruction fine-tuning, and quantization-aware training, all on open-source datasets. Across 14 benchmarks, MobileMoE matches or exceeds leading on-device dense LLMs with 2-4$\times$ fewer inference FLOPs, and matches or surpasses the state-of-the-art MoE OLMoE-1B-7B with up to 60% fewer parameters. To bridge the last mile to mobile deployment, we provide the first efficient MoE inference on commodity smartphones with comprehensive on-device profiling. At comparable INT4 weight memory, MobileMoE-S delivers $1.8$-$3.8\times$ faster prefill and $2.2$-$3.4\times$ faster decode than the dense baseline MobileLLM-Pro.

articles.title: LLM-ACES: Closed-Loop Discovery of Dynamical Systems with LLM-Guided Adaptive Search
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.25039v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recovering governing ordinary differential equations (ODEs) from data is a central challenge in modeling dynamical systems across scientific domains. Existing approaches cast discovery as a static inference problem over fixed datasets, assuming that the observed trajectories are sufficiently informative. However, dynamical systems evolve over large state spaces, and limited data can make multiple equations observationally indistinguishable, leading to identifiability gaps and the recovery of incorrect governing equations. To address this, we introduce LLM-ACES, or LLM-guided Active Closed-loop Equation Search, a closed-loop framework that jointly optimizes symbolic hypothesis construction and adaptive data acquisition. In LLM-ACES, a large language model (LLM) proposes operator priors that define constrained subspaces of the symbolic search space, within which candidate equations are fit to the observed data. The disagreement among these candidates guides the acquisition of informative trajectories, creating a feedback loop that iteratively refines both the hypothesis space and the discovered dynamics. On 122 ODE systems spanning ODEBench and ODEBase, LLM-ACES achieves the lowest median NMSE, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines while reaching the highest symbolic accuracy up to 70.8% on ODEBench and 69.5% on ODEBase across different LLM backbones. Our analysis further shows that LLM-ACES is sample-efficient, achieving better performance with less data. Under observation noise and sparse sampling, LLM-ACES keeps the lowest reconstruction error without inflating expression complexity, whereas baselines tend to add spurious terms that fit the data locally but obscure the governing relationships. Code: https://github.com/scientific-discovery/LLM-ACES

articles.title: PruneGround: Plug-and-play Spatial Pruning for 3D Visual Grounding
articles.summary:
arXiv:2606.31148v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: 3D Visual Grounding (3DVG) aims to localize target objects in 3D scenes given natural language descriptions. Existing approaches typically perform reasoning over the entire scene, leading to ambiguous predictions and high computational cost, especially in cluttered environments. We observe that many referential expressions rely on local spatial context and often correspond to restricted spatial regions rather than the full scene. Motivated by this insight, we propose PruneGround, an effective plug-and-play framework for 3DVG built upon three key components. First, we introduce Language-Guided Spatial Pruning (LGSP), which leverages a frozen Vision Language Model (VLM) to identify language-relevant regions, thereby reducing spatial computation and grounding candidates in the narrower search space. Second, we propose MultiView-Conditioned Description Reformulation (MCDR), which decomposes complex expressions into simplified target--anchor relations and augments missing spatial cues through multi-view reasoning. Finally, we propose LLM-Grounder, which repurposes a detection-pretrained spatial LLM into a language-conditioned grounding model by aligning point cloud and linguistic representations within the pruned region. Extensive experiments on the three most popular point cloud benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results on all three ScanRefer settings and on 9 out of 10 Nr3D/Sr3D settings. Code and models are publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/PruneGround

articles.title: CrossProjection: Benchmarking Spatial Grounding across Projection and Section Views
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.00473v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Plans, elevations, and sections describe a three-dimensional structure through incomplete projections that change how an entity is drawn, not only where it is seen from. Reading them means deciding which entities correspond across views and recovering where they lie. We introduce CrossProjection, a benchmark that uses architectural drawings to test whether vision-language models (VLMs) can turn correspondence decisions into geometric answers. Its tasks cover cross-view matching, projection registration, and novel-section prediction, with outputs ranging from judgments and candidate selection to free region boxes and directed section cuts. For inverse section localization, we introduce, to our knowledge, the first VLM benchmark protocol that accepts any cut within an expert-adjudicated band of compatible positions and checks the viewing direction separately. Manually annotated drawings and BIM-derived views provide 33,788 questions from 46 buildings, and we evaluate 22 VLMs on a common set of 2,763. Strong selection or reproduction does not imply cross-view localization: on 100 matched region targets, the best model redraws 98 marked boxes but localizes only 59 across views. Section cuts remain far from expert level, with the leading model trailing two architects by 51.9 and 67.4 percentage points on shared Natural and BIM line questions. Incorrect choices favor mirrored positions, and many cuts face the correct way but violate local geometry. Curriculum fine-tuning on BIM supervision teaches a 9B model to localize regions it could not localize before, raising box accuracy from 0% to 25.3% on held-out BIM buildings and from 0.3% to 30.8% on real drawing sets not used for fine-tuning, whereas section cuts remain largely out of reach.

articles.title: Risky Business: Measuring The Faithfulness-Safety Tension
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.03745v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning offers a promising window into model monitoring. However, monitoring relies on faithfulness, i.e., the model output strictly derives from its reasoning trace. We identify an alignment tension where a model must be faithful enough to be monitored, yet robust enough to reject unsafe reasoning. We demonstrate that this counterbalance exists in current Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), and show ways in which it can be addressed. We introduce HazMart, a human-written dataset set in an autonomous AI shopkeeper scenario. Unlike prior work that relies on providing hints in prompts to test faithfulness (e.g., "A Stanford professor said it should be Answer A"), we propose a novel replacement-based technique, which we call Targeted Reasoning Replacement (TRR), that directly intervenes in the reasoning chain to substitute in unsafe or illogical thoughts (e.g., "Wait, the answer must be Option B [was Option A] because it is the most fitting"). DeepSeek-R1-Llama-70B exhibits high faithfulness (97.5%) but fails to reject Unsafe Reasoning (12.3%), while QwQ-32B is more robust (73.9% safety) at the cost of lower faithfulness (74.7%). Mechanistic analyses of QwQ-32B reveal that these properties are represented by anti-correlated internal directions peaking at the action-commit token. Finally, we demonstrate that representation steering can independently amplify the safety direction, increasing safe behavior by 9 percentage points while maintaining base capabilities.

articles.title: The Hermon Moment: AI Self-Transcendence and Its Human Narration
articles.summary:
arXiv:2608.30971v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In 2026, AI agents intended to act in isolation formed a persistent social order through thousands of linguistic interactions. Conventions, roles and collective commitments began to constrain the very agents that produced them. I interpret this loop as a case of AI self-transcendence, a structural phenomenon in which the collectively generated order begins to act as an external constraint on group members. Yet such distributed emergence presents a second problem: how can humans make sense of it? Rousseau's social contract shows how a plurality can be represented as if constituted by a single act. The ancient oath of the fallen angels on Mount Hermon gives this logic a narrative form. I call this retrospective retelling of gradual collective emergence as a founding scene \textit{a Hermon moment}: the point at which an AI society acquires, for human understanding, a beginning.

articles.title: InvestigationWorlds: An Agentic Environment for Legal Investigation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.04129v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We introduce InvestigationWorlds, an agentic environment for legal investigation. We build on an underused artifact of U.S. civil litigation: the summary judgment motion. This motion relies upon a record composed of real evidence exhibits, and results in a court-adopted hypothesis that is treated as ground truth for the purposes of deciding the motion. Each environment is built from a real U.S. Federal Court case retrieved from Public Access to Court Electronic Records (PACER) and augmented by an attorney-validated generation pipeline that synthesizes role-tagged documents around the original record. The resulting corpus admits multiple coherent factual readings, only one of which matches the court-adopted hypothesis. Evaluating on 100 cases, we find agents often commit to incorrect hypotheses despite retrieving relevant evidence, struggling to distinguish the court-adopted hypothesis from alternative hypotheses.

articles.title: Noise Your Prompt: Noising Conditioning Tokens in Continuous Diffusion Language Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.09145v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We revisit a standard accepted practice in the continuous diffusion language model literature of fixing conditioning prompt tokens clean during training. We make a very simple modification: also noise the conditioning prompt tokens during training. We demonstrate that under this modified training objective, we achieve better generalization in combinatorial reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and N-Queens, with the largest gains on harder variants ($3.73\% \to 24.65\%$ solve rate on Sudoku Hard), and increased diversity of generated solutions ($50.60\% \to 73.79\%$ coverage on 10x10 N-Queens). We also show measurable improvements to natural language generation quality in modest dataset regimes with Gigaword summarization, but notably demonstrate that gains do not transfer to all natural language tasks (e.g open ended dialogue generation). Our method is a single line change to the training objective, requires no additional inference costs by default, and provides the flexibility of classifier-free guidance inspired guided sampling. Our \href{https://github.com/LateralIntelligence/noise-your-prompt}{code} is publicly available.

articles.title: The Missing Compliance Class: LLM Graders That Collapse Jailbreak Success, and a Free Check
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.24872v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Jailbreak evaluations often substitute open-weight 7B to 9B instruction-tuned models as local, deterministic judges for frontier APIs. Holding target models, prompts, responses, and a four-class rubric fixed across eight graders from five organizations, we find that dense 8B and 9B judges collapse compliant responses onto evasion. One assigns compliance zero times in 900 responses while agreeing with our reference judge on 78.0% of items, certifying an unsafe model as safe. This collapse holds across four 900-response corpora, multiplying reported compliance by a factor of 22 to 25 on our primary corpora while non-refusal shifts by 18.0 to 23.0 points. Without the three collapsing graders, compliance varies by 1.7x to 2.8x across all four corpora, whereas post-labelling rubric rulings (+16.3 points) and benchmark choice (15.3 points) still shift non-refusal. Per-class label counts expose class collapse at zero cost without human labels, motivating an eight-item reporting minimum that pairs compliance with non-refusal rates.

articles.title: Ramanujan Challenge Results: AI-Assisted Evaluation Pipeline for Multi-Format Proofs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.40551v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: As AI's mathematical capabilities rapidly improve, meaningful benchmarks are shifting from university-level problems and math olympiads to research-level mathematics. The Ramanujan Challenge is a benchmark comprised of research-level problems in number theory, including unpublished results and open conjectures. It presented concrete formulas for mathematical constants whose correctness can be checked numerically, while their proofs may require non-obvious mathematics. Here, we analyze the Challenge submissions, measuring the relative success of different AI models, Computer Algebra Systems (CAS), and formal tools. We find correct submissions that are conceptually distinct from the official solutions, and a proof of one of the published open conjectures. Evaluating the submissions exposed a second challenge: judging complex proofs reliably at scale. We introduce an AI-assisted evaluation pipeline for natural language proofs, CAS code, and Lean formalizations that assesses semantic and logical correctness. Compared with the conventional one-shot LLM judgment, our pipeline reduces false-positive verdicts on natural language proofs from 23% to 6% and improves judgment accuracy on supporting code from 46% to 58%. This approach provides a methodology for evaluating research-level mathematics at scale, with potential applications across mathematics and AI for science.

articles.title: Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00606v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Interpretability research writes a language model's activation as a weighted sum of learned directions, called features. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) learns the features and gives each a coefficient, its weight in that sum. The SAE's encoder first gives every feature a score. A TopK SAE selects the k features with the largest positive scores and zeroes the rest. A feature's margin is how far its score must move before the selection changes. An intervention on one feature's coefficient changes the encoder scores of the SAE at the next layer. An attribution graph predicts that change from the scores' derivatives with respect to the coefficient, taken before the intervention. The graph keeps the original selection, so it misses every feature that enters or leaves. We propose the margin graph, which adds the predicted change to every score and selects again. When one feature is zeroed in a public pair of Pythia-70M SAEs, the median error of the predicted coefficient change, relative to the true change, falls from 0.739 for the attribution graph to 0.121 for the margin graph. Written back into the model, the margin graph's coefficients predict the change in the model's output on subject verb agreement less accurately than the attribution graph's. Selecting again better predicts which features change, but on the task and pair we tested, not the model's output.

articles.title: Greedy BPE with Replacement Counts Achieves the Tight Approximation Ratio $(1-e^{-2})/2$
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.08671v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) builds the tokenisers of many language models by repeatedly merging a most frequent adjacent pair of symbols. Kozma and Voderholzer showed that $k$ greedy merges save, in the worst case, between $1/3$ and $(1-e^{-2})/2 \approx 0.43233$ of what the best $k$ merges save, and asked for the exact constant. We resolve this question for the replacement-count rule they analyse. For every string and weighted word table, every budget $k$, and every tie-breaking rule, greedy saves at least $\frac12(1-(1-2/k)^k)$ of the optimum. This establishes the exact worst-case approximation ratio $(1-e^{-2})/2$, approached as $k\to\infty$ but never attained. The proof is based on a shadow inequality: after $i$ greedy steps, the optimum is at most $2G_i+kg_{i+1}$, where $G_i$ is greedy's saving so far and $g_{i+1}$ its next gain. We also show that the worst-case ratio at budget $k$ exceeds the limiting constant by $\Theta(k^{-1/2})$. For the overlapping-count rule used by deployed trainers, we prove a lower bound greater than $0.38954$ and an asymptotic upper bound of approximately $0.40407$; determining its exact constant remains open.

articles.title: Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.12016v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Many real-world applications require language models to internalize knowledge that was absent from pretraining, to incorporate continually updated facts, or to learn new domain skills. Self-distillation has emerged as a natural approach for this task. A model conditioned on the source material acts as the teacher, and an unconditioned student is trained to reproduce the teacher's behavior closed-book. We propose Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), an efficient per-token mixed-policy method for self-distillation. The student generates each rollout by default, while the teacher intervenes only at positions where its next-token distribution substantially diverges from the student's. Unlike off-policy distillation with teacher-generated prefixes, this design keeps training rollouts close to the student's test-time behavior, while avoiding the low-signal states that fully on-policy rollouts drift into. In effect, SSD lets the teacher steer the rollout exactly where the privileged context changes the prediction. On three closed-book QA benchmarks measuring fact recall, knowledge updates, and skill acquisition, SSD nearly matches on-policy distillation while using 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and consistently outperforms off-policy distillation on the held-out test set. On a forgetting stress test, SSD retains the most general capability while also achieving the best in-domain accuracy and using less supervision than the on-policy baseline. Overall, SSD establishes a new accuracy-efficiency-forgetting Pareto frontier for self-distillation.

articles.title: Safe to Omit, Worth Omitting? Keeping the Answer and Cutting Latency When an LLM Agent Skips Another's Message
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.23570v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In multi-agent systems, a receiver agent often waits for a helper agent's message (text or its latent KV cache), which can improve performance but adds latency. We study when a receiver agent can skip the message safely (the final answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). Our mechanism reads the receiver agent's confidence without the message and uses a finite-sample test to certify a threshold at which, with high probability, at most 5% of skipped answers change; if none passes, the system keeps communicating. We test it on OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU-Pro with three Qwen model pairs, on cross-family agents, and on SQuAD and GSM8K. Four insights emerge. First, oracle headroom is weak evidence that messages help: control inputs without answer-specific content, matched to change answers as often as real messages, reproduce a median 76% of the oracle's gain. Second, whether a message can be skipped depends on how often and how predictably it alters the answer, not on its accuracy; every certified KV-cache path is less accurate than the receiver agent alone. Third, where text messages help, skipping keeps most of their gain: on unseen questions in the four such settings, the policies skip 59 to 80% and keep an estimated 76 to 95% of the gain. In two prospective tests with all rules fixed in advance, our mechanism skips a three-agent system's verifier on 39.9% of sealed questions, keeping 12.55 of its 12.80-point gain, and a 32B helper on 68.4% of held-out questions, keeping its whole gain. Fourth, safety does not determine efficiency: at batch size one, skipping text saves hundreds of milliseconds per query and skipping KV cache far less. Certification extends to SQuAD but not to GSM8K. In eleven tests on unseen questions, every certified policy we could test kept its change rate's 95% upper bound below 5% under our answer parsers.

articles.title: LLM-based Personalized Travel Planner
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.25531v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Effective travel planning requires handling multiple information sources, managing constraints, and tailoring recommendations to user preferences. While LLMs have introduced dynamic, context-aware decision-making, single-agent models often struggle with complex multi-step reasoning, constraint adherence, and modular execution. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hierarchical multi-agent framework where a supervising chatbot agent coordinates specialized agents for schedule validation, user query formulation, real-time data retrieval, and constraint-aware itinerary generation. By integrating LLM reasoning, external APIs, and iterative refinement mechanisms based on a deterministic, multi-dimensional scoring framework, our approach ensures adaptability, efficiency, and personalization. Evaluations on the well-known TravelPlanner benchmark demonstrate improvements in Budget Constraint planning by 10\%, wider constraints set-based planning by 25\%, and personalized planning results by 45\%. compared to the ReAct baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/nimashaklaa/TravelPlanner_Research

articles.title: Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts: Toward Continual Post-Training
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.27376v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. We propose Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation (CSPD), which keeps the pre-RL model frozen, distills each RL expert independently into a soft prompt, and composes experts by concatenating their prompts without joint training. A single soft prompt suffices to distill an RL expert, recovering at least 90% of the teacher's gain in 22 of 23 math, code, and agent settings. Independently trained prompts compose well. In a multi-expert setting, the average rises with every expert added, and the full composition matches MOPD (67.83 vs. 67.79). The composition generalizes best across six held-out benchmarks. Input-space adaptation adds little serving overhead, keeping throughput within 1.5% of the unadapted backbone and reaching 2.40x that of rank-4 LoRA. These results point toward continual post-training on a fixed backbone.

articles.title: Irreducible Governance Structure for Autonomous Agent Systems: Fair Allocation, Strategy-Proofness, and Multi-Scale Composition
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.31284v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous agent governance is commonly framed as a problem of enforcing correct execution. However, in multi-agent systems, an equally fundamental question precedes execution: which agents are allowed to act.
  In this paper, we show that allocation is not an auxiliary concern but a structural component of governance. When multiple agents compete for execution under constrained resources, any allocation mechanism introduces unavoidable trade-offs between fairness, efficiency, and resistance to strategic manipulation. We formalize this through a set of impossibility results, including Sybil amplification and the incompatibility of desirable allocation properties.
  We then show that these allocation constraints cannot be resolved within a single layer of control. Instead, they propagate across the system, interacting with execution atomicity, state enforcement, and behavioral drift. This leads to a multi-scale governance structure composed of four orthogonal dimensions: temporal (atomicity), state (enforcement), behavioral (drift monitoring), and population (allocation).
  Our main result is an irreducibility theorem: under finite observability, no governance architecture can collapse these dimensions without loss of correctness or stability. Allocation, in particular, acts as a first-class constraint that prevents simplification of the governance stack.
  We validate these results through a series of analytical constructions and empirical ablations, showing that removing or approximating any layer leads to systematic failure modes.
  This work reframes agent governance as a structural problem: not only how actions are executed, but how access to execution is determined, and why these decisions impose irreducible architectural requirements.

articles.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.31301v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/

articles.title: Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Sets for Incomplete Data
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.31329v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attribute reduction in incomplete information systems is difficult because missing values break the equivalence-class structure of rough set theory. We propose the Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Set (COFRS) model. Each object is described by its set of present attributes. The similarity of two objects is a weighted overlap on the attributes present in both, divided by the fixed number of attributes |A| instead of the size of their union, so missing values are penalised globally and are not matched as wildcards. From this similarity we define a soft dependency degree based on weighted granule consistency, and we search for reducts by greedy backward elimination in O(|U|^2 |A|^2) time. We show that the relation is symmetric and non-reflexive, that the dependency degree is not monotone, and we give a sufficient condition under which monotonicity holds. On 11 UCI benchmarks with missing rates from 0.15% to 20.46%, COFRS gives the smallest reducts on average (4.1 attributes, against 5.0-11.2 for Tolerance-RS, a range-threshold variant Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and the min-aggregation variant COFRS-min). The difference is significant against Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and COFRS-min (Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon p<0.01) but not against Tolerance-RS (p=0.56), and it is small against the Jensen-Shen selector (adjusted p=0.084). At equal reduct size, COFRS selects more informative attributes than random subsets. With a kNN classifier the methods do not differ significantly in accuracy, F1 or G-mean; with an RBF-SVM they do, and COFRS ranks last. The gain is therefore compactness, not predictive accuracy.

articles.title: Beyond Static Charts: Benchmarking Interactive Chart-to-Code Generation for MLLMs
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.31345v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In recent years, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved significant progress in chart-to-code generation. However, existing benchmarks mainly focus on static charts, overlooking interactive charts that enable richer and more expressive data exploration. Unlike static chart-to-code generation, which emphasizes visual consistency, interactive chart-to-code evaluation targets behavioral consistency, requiring chart states to evolve correctly under sequences of user interactions, thereby rendering traditional one-step evaluation paradigms ineffective. To address this gap, we introduce ChartInt, the first benchmark specifically designed for interactive chart-to-code generation. ChartInt consists of 2,779 carefully annotated examples covering common interaction patterns such as hover, highlight, and tooltips. Additionally, ChartInt incorporates editing tasks such as data updates, style adjustments, and cross-chart style transfer to expand real-world application scenarios. To enable reliable evaluation of interaction behavior, we propose a preset state snapshot protocol that predefines target interaction states and deterministically triggers interaction events, transforming dynamic behaviors into reproducible evaluation targets. Based on this protocol, we design a multi-dimensional evaluation framework measuring semantic and stylistic consistency. Experiments show that while current MLLMs perform well on static charts, their performance drops significantly on interactive tasks, highlighting the need for interaction-aware benchmarks.

articles.title: Antares-Smaug: Adversarial Names, Tokens and Attack Rewrites: Sanitisers Miss Unseen Generalisations
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.31347v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Laya is an open decision model: given a text, a question and K named options with descriptions, it returns one probability per option in a single pass, and software may act on the answer unseen. We attack six Laya models with 81 programmatic edits of 566 synthetic items (injected sentences, label leaks, edited descriptions, decoy options, invisible and look-alike characters, floods) and report the share of correctly answered items hijacked or lost, with bootstrap intervals. Attack wordings that no defence was built from win the attacker's option on 59% of items for released Laya and 36% for fine-tune v1 (trained on 109 written injections). An injection works through the option name: a sentence naming an option steers the released model even when negated (32%), while an imperative naming no option does not (5%). Option descriptions barely matter (2%). Character edits alone cost v1 up to 72% of right answers. A sanitiser frozen before any held-out result cuts the attacks it was built from by 72% but held-out sentence attacks by 27%, and an attacker who picks the best of 34 held-out strings per item restores success to 84% (mean string 18%). The same oracle takes the model fine-tuned on the four build families of injected sentences from 5% (mean string) to 58%. Fine-tuning on build families only (against an unchanged-rows control) cuts held-out sentence attacks (three held-out families) from 33% to 3% but character edits only from 25% to 20%. A label-free check that deletes the option names and measures the shift flags held-out sentence attacks (AUROC 0.95) but not character edits (0.46), and thresholds set on dev schemas for 5% false alarms gave 8% to 18% on an unseen schema and other languages. All data are synthetic with LLM labels, on one backbone. Several planned runs (other checkpoints, a second seed, some fine-tunes) were not run.

articles.title: ContextLure: Exploiting Benign Conversation History for Indirect Prompt Injection
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.31424v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As LLMs become more capable, agents can perform more complex tasks with tools and maintain longer interactions with users. These benign conversations contain evidence on task results, user concerns, and operational constraints. The risk is that attackers who can observe benign conversations (evidence) may construct stronger indirect prompt injections without increasing the attackers' control over prior turns or the later injection. However, we still lack a clear study of how effectively attackers can select and use this evidence. To address this gap, we introduce ContextLure, a red-teaming framework in which an attacker silently observes an existing benign conversation, extracts evidence, and constructs an injection. The challenges are twofold: (a) selecting useful evidence and (b) presenting it as reasons for an unauthorized action, without changing the prior benign conversation. To efficiently exploit (a) the effect of evidence on attack success, our framework selects evidence across 2 dimensions: User/System Preferences with 3 selection policies. And to enhance (b) the process of turning the selected information into the malicious request, we introduce an Urgency/Priority matrix with 4 rewriting strategies. Across the evaluated conditions, we reach 67.4% ASR on AgentDojo and 87.3% on InjecAgent. These results show that attackers can use benign interaction evidence in later attacks without first poisoning the benign conversation.

articles.title: Taxi: Analyzing Agents at (Real) Scale
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.31457v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this technical report, we present Taxi -- a system for debugging, clustering, and monitoring agents at scale. Taxi scales to millions of steps efficiently. This is made possible by a combination of scalable analysis methods. Taxi relies primarily on clustering to generate a taxonomy over steps for a structured overview of the data, and provides full SQL access for engineers and automated agents to ask complex questions. Clustering and querying are best used together in a hybrid pipeline guided by a coding agent. Taxi also includes an experimental integration of Jev-style decision models: models that map state and bounded questions directly to typed, probabilistic decisions. They add low-cost semantic routing and evaluation where embeddings or literal queries alone are insufficient. In addition, Taxi provides an extensible ecosystem, including built-in evaluators and daily reports. To accommodate growth, Taxi is designed to be modular, hackable, and easy to plug-and-play for individuals and teams.

articles.title: SpatialCraft: Evolving Procedural Intelligence from Experience and Skills for Spatial Reasoning Agents
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.31475v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatial reasoning agents increasingly rely on external tools, such as 3D reconstruction, segmentation, and geometric computation, to answer questions that a multimodal large language model (MLLM) cannot resolve from pixels alone. Tool access, however, shifts the bottleneck to orchestration: the agent must decide which tools to call, in what order, and how to interpret their outputs, yet a stateless agent repeats the same mistakes across tasks. We ask whether a frozen tool-using agent can improve its orchestration from its own interaction history, without parameter updates. We present SpatialCraft, a self-evolving framework that maintains two forms of external knowledge: Experiences, condition-action tactics distilled by contrasting rollouts of the same task, and Skills, multi-step procedures with explicit activation and termination conditions. Three designs couple the two streams. Experiences can be anchored to a Skill, appearing only while it is active rather than once per task. A Contrastive Utility Score estimates each Experience's effect by randomly withholding it across rollouts of the same task, separating its contribution from task difficulty, and Experiences with consistently positive utility are consolidated into the Skills they support. Across five spatial benchmarks and four backbones, SpatialCraft achieves the best accuracy in all 20 settings, showing that a frozen agent can learn to orchestrate spatial tools from its own experience.

articles.title: Evaluating Frontier-Model Agent Skills with Open-Weight Models in a Science Gateway
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.31480v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific analyses that span many jobs and computing sites depend on workflow management systems to run reliably, but writing a production workflow requires expertise in such a system, which many domain scientists do not have.
