Abstract: Anomaly detection in medical images is a complex task, requiring the development of a robust model using only healthy patient data. Without access to labeled data, modern approaches typically employ self-supervised learning to obtain a model of normality. Since world models promise to build strong internal representations of their environment, we consider them as suitable candidates for the medical anomaly detection environment, namely medical investigations of healthy patients. To this end, we propose MADJEPA, a medical anomaly detector based on an enhanced multi-stage joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). We design a multi-stage training pipeline to produce a robust detector: (1) image-based JEPA (I-JEPA) training aims to learn a strong representation of normal training data; (2) target encoder distillation aims to modulate over-generalization of I-JEPA representations to abnormal data; (3) pseudo-anomaly classification aims to calibrate anomaly predictions by learning a tight boundary around the normal data manifold. To demonstrate our design, we carry out comprehensive experiments on six datasets covering various medical image domains (e.g. MRI, OCT, X-ray, histopathology), comparing our MADJEPA with numerous state-of-the-art methods. The results show that our carefully designed world model, MADJEPA, attains competitive results, ranking first on three datasets. Our ablation studies further confirm the utility of each training stage, indicating that I-JEPA alone is not sufficient to obtain competitive results in medical anomaly detection. We publicly release our code at https://github.com/Sabina085/madjepa.

articles.title: Bradley-Terry Training Can Distort Outcome Probabilities of Initially Accurate Language World Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.25594v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Comparative feedback, in which a judge says which of two candidate outcomes is closer to what happened, is a practical way to train language world models that assign probabilities to an action's outcomes. We show that, fitted with a Bradley-Terry objective, it need not teach the true outcome probabilities and can distort accurate ones. On a simulated robot push with enumerated outcome distributions, this objective takes a model that is accurate on unseen layouts (hazard error 2.4 percentage points, pp) and moves 33 to 43 pp of its probability onto outcomes that none of a condition's enumerated branches produces. The cause is the objective, not the comparisons: its optimum, computed before training, predicts where the model ends up, and a likelihood that knows the judge's rule learns from the same comparisons without the shift. The shift is robust: it recurs on unseen conditions, under five candidate laws and a three-fold denser enumeration, and about 29 pp remain without the physically impossible events. Its cost is conditional: with those events it inflates hazard probabilities, and a threshold inherited from the pre-feedback model costs about 3 pp of utility per decision on trained and 1 to 2 pp on unseen conditions, through false rejects; without them the utility loss averages below 1 pp over six seeds, though a small regret in action choice remains. Audits of readout, response and decision trace the effect from probabilities to actions.

articles.title: VMSA: Video Memory Skill Agent for Long Video Understanding
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.27381v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Long-video question answering requires retrieving and integrating relevant evidence from videos spanning hours or even days. Recent agentic approaches organize video information into external memories and iteratively retrieve evidence to answer questions. However, effective retrieval and reasoning remain challenging, as agents must determine what information to search for, which memory sources to access, and how to connect evidence across distant temporal intervals. To address these challenges, we propose Video Memory Skill Agent (VMSA), a framework that jointly designs structured video memories and memory skills for long-video understanding. VMSA constructs three complementary memory components. Segment Caption Memory and Entity Event Memory serve as searchable evidence sources, while Entity-Aware Episode Memory provides broad yet detailed video context to guide evidence retrieval and reasoning. To further support effective memory utilization, VMSA induces memory skills from successful agent trajectories, incrementally refining or extending a compact skill library to guide iterative evidence retrieval, reasoning, and verification. Across seven long-video question-answering benchmarks, VMSA achieves the highest accuracy on all three week-long egocentric benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.4% on Ego-R1 Bench, and the best or competitive performance on four additional benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of all three memory components and memory skills, with memory skills also improving temporal evidence localization.

articles.title: Self-Supervised Continuous-Time Depth Learning and Ego-Motion Estimation from Asynchronous Events
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.27509v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Event cameras register brightness changes pixel by pixel with microsecond precision, whereas the dense depth that could supervise them is costly to acquire and exists only at isolated instants. Condensing the stream into frames eases learning, but at the expense of the very timing that sets event sensing apart. We propose a self-supervised approach in which each event is assigned its own depth in continuous time, and the camera motion is recovered from the same observations. Supervision arises from geometry: lifted into 3D by its predicted depth and displaced by the camera motion at the instant it fired, an event should coincide with others produced by the same edge, so any misalignment exposes an error in depth or motion. Differentiable rendering then turns these per-event estimates into dense depth maps at target times within each window, faithful to the events behind them. On MVSEC, the approach outperforms prior event-only self-supervised methods in most sequences and depth ranges, with the widest margins at night, and recovers camera rotation more accurately than an earlier unsupervised event-based method. Ablations isolate the roles of local spatiotemporal context, the temporal backbone, and the alignment objective. These results position motion-compensated event alignment as a principled source of supervision for continuous-time depth and ego-motion estimation.

articles.title: Social sycophancy differs across access modes of large language models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.28012v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can display sycophancy, a tendency to excessively praise, agree with, or validate a user. Existing studies have tested LLMs for sycophancy primarily through application programming interfaces (APIs) rather than the consumer user interfaces (UIs) through which the public commonly interacts with LLMs. Access mode (API vs. UI) may affect observed sycophancy rates. However, it remains unknown to what extent prominent models show API-UI differences in social sycophancy, which includes behaviors potentially more likely in UIs (e.g., softening warranted criticism). We tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek through both APIs and UIs on four dimensions of social sycophancy. Across models, UI access was generally associated with greater social sycophancy, with odds ratios up to 7.56 (95% CI [6.22, 9.20]). However, UI-API differences varied significantly across models for all sycophancy dimensions, including a pronounced reversal for DeepSeek moral sycophancy (43% UI vs. 82.3% API). Overall, our results suggest that API-based LLM evaluations may underestimate the prevalence of sycophancy in corresponding consumer-facing systems, making access conditions consequential for the external validity of LLM evaluation. To facilitate research on access-mode effects, we release 57,000 model responses and SycoUI, a browser-automation pipeline for standardized cross-interface LLM evaluation.

articles.title: Seeing vs. Knowing: Counterfactual Supervision and Correction for 3D-Aware Object Editing
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.29542v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Rotating, translating, or rescaling an object in a photograph requires revealing unseen surfaces, preserving visible appearance, and updating shadows and reflections. Reconstructed 3D assets, rendered at the target pose as a 3D state, provide explicit geometric guidance, but their imperfect textures may conflict with the photograph, while standard paired training does not explicitly teach the editor which source to trust. To address this, we propose counterfactual state supervision, which constructs controlled photo--state conflicts through hidden-surface repainting, hidden geometry with re-rendered shadows and reflections, and visible-surface texture replacement. This teaches the editor to follow the 3D state for unseen content while preserving photograph-visible appearance. However, learning this distinction does not ensure that it is maintained during sampling. We therefore introduce symmetric counterfactual correction, which uses state-side and photo-side twins, which share the photograph and the state respectively, to construct directed latent perturbations toward condition-inconsistent targets and train recovery toward the target specified by the current condition. Both strategies operate only during training, requiring no architectural changes or additional inference steps. Experiments on OBJect and SpatialEdit-Bench demonstrate strong spatial editing performance and content preservation, while controlled ablations show improved source selection and sustained responsiveness to conditioning during sampling.

articles.title: PixelOne: From Options to Pixels in a Single Forward for GUI Grounding
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.30235v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: GUI grounding requires precise clicks at low latency. Recent models such as GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift predict coordinates in one forward pass using fixed global bins with local refinement. However, screenshot downsampling removes detail needed to locate small controls, while fixed bins cover larger pixel ranges at higher resolutions. We introduce PixelOne, which transfers spatial knowledge from a search teacher to a student that predicts clicks directly from screenshots at native resolution. The teacher uses VideoJEV's text-option scorer to select rows and columns and progressively zoom into candidate regions. The student inherits the teacher's parameters and matches its distributions over explored regions through spatial distillation alongside box supervision. At inference, the same decision head selects a visual token, and a lightweight pixel head predicts the click within it, all in one forward pass. A click-aligned loss encourages pixels inside the target box to score above those outside. Across four benchmarks, PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B achieves 83.8% mean accuracy, the highest among the evaluated single-forward grounders, with a mean latency of 0.43 s per target.

articles.title: De Novo Generation of Odorant Molecules with Targeted Olfactory Receptor Activation Patterns
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.30509v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Odor perception arises from a combinatorial code in which each molecule activates a specific subset of olfactory receptors (ORs), and the resulting activation pattern determines the perceived smell. We present a framework for de novo generation of molecules predicted to match target multi-receptor activation profiles. We first construct a panoramic binding matrix over 20 ORs, then cluster it to discover representative activation patterns, and finally formulate a structured selectivity loss, combining pairwise ranking, distribution matching, and complexity constraints, to steer a molecular generator via reinforcement learning. Across nine target profiles of varying complexity, our method achieves high predicted selectivity within 18000 oracle calls and provides the largest gains on profiles that are rare under the prior, especially broad-spectrum and sparse-activator targets.

articles.title: RoboInF: A Benchmark for Instruction Fidelity in Robotic Manipulation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.30555v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution. Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes. Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions. We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction. For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution. The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact. We evaluate leading manipulation policies ($\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash). All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.

articles.title: Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.30986v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Forward diffusion reinforcement learning (RL)---enabling deterministic ODE sampling without trajectory backpropagation---has grown increasingly popular for efficiently aligning diffusion models. However, we reveal that existing methods essentially rely on signed reward-weighted regression (RWR), regressing the trainable policy velocity onto rollouts from a behavior distribution. Unbiased baseline subtraction implicitly assumes that the policy velocity equals the behavior marginal velocity---an idealized assumption violated under classifier-free guidance (CFG) rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, and imperfect online self-consistency. This behavior--policy mismatch breaks baseline invariance and injects baseline-induced gradient drift, destabilizing training. To resolve this issue, we propose Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching (iTDM), taking the infinitesimal limit of Trajectory Distribution Matching toward a time-local reward-guided target via the posterior-score identity to yield a sample-level gradient anchored at the behavior velocity without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. Tracking this velocity with an online auxiliary denoiser guarantees exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum, effectively suppressing baseline drift across both online and offline RL. Extensive experiments across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment show that iTDM achieves state-of-the-art in-domain and out-of-domain performance across group-wise online/offline RL and pairwise offline RL. Notably, on the challenging GenEval2 benchmark, iTDM converges nearly 3\times faster than competing methods while scaling smoothly to 0.87 without collapse. Furthermore, iTDM scales effectively to the 5.6B FLUX.3 model, achieving better performance across both in-domain and unseen metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/Luo-Yihong/iTDM

Then I noticed the scheduled tasks in ChatGPT/Grok Bot/etc. also use up a lot of your plan's allowance, often on checks that find nothing new. articles.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
articles.summary: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. Fable class models in June/July We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release , due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them. In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work. After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st. For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models . My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive , after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug. A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm. Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook. I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well. These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model. 3D modeling and game development in September/October Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for. I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example. 3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa. Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game . It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play. I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play! Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked . My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay. Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time. Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games. The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster . It feels like another inflection point to me. Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too? I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement. I'm getting so much done with that model right now! It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42 , 1.0a43 , and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37 , 0.37.1 , 0.37.2 , 0.37.3 , and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks , represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements. If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it . That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks. Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand. articles.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
articles.summary: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries: With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library . It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. Here's the digitized sketchbook . Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work. Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue ? Mark thinks it will be mild: But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature. Tags: history , ai , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-search , deep-blue , gpt-6-astra

articles.title: Video generation models as world simulators
articles.summary: We explore large-scale training of generative models on video data. Specifically, we train text-conditional diffusion models jointly on videos and images of variable durations, resolutions and aspect ratios. We leverage a transformer architecture that operates on spacetime patches of video and image latent codes. Our largest model, Sora, is capable of generating a minute of high fidelity video. Our results suggest that scaling video generation models is a promising path towards building general purpose simulators of the physical world.

articles.title: Improving mathematical reasoning with process supervision
articles.summary: We’ve trained a model to achieve a new state-of-the-art in mathematical problem solving by rewarding each correct step of reasoning (“process supervision”) instead of simply rewarding the correct final answer (“outcome supervision”). In addition to boosting performance relative to outcome supervision, process supervision also has an important alignment benefit: it directly trains the model to produce a chain-of-thought that is endorsed by humans.

articles.title: Forecasting potential misuses of language models for disinformation campaigns and how to reduce risk
articles.summary: OpenAI researchers collaborated with Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology and the Stanford Internet Observatory to investigate how large language models might be misused for disinformation purposes. The collaboration included an October 2021 workshop bringing together 30 disinformation researchers, machine learning experts, and policy analysts, and culminated in a co-authored report building on more than a year of research. This report outlines the threats that language models pose to the information environment if used to augment disinformation campaigns and introduces a framework for analyzing potential mitigations. Read the full report here.

articles.title: Learning to play Minecraft with Video PreTraining
articles.summary: We trained a neural network to play Minecraft by Video PreTraining (VPT) on a massive unlabeled video dataset of human Minecraft play, while using only a small amount of labeled contractor data. With fine-tuning, our model can learn to craft diamond tools, a task that usually takes proficient humans over 20 minutes (24,000 actions). Our model uses the native human interface of keypresses and mouse movements, making it quite general, and represents a step towards general computer-using agents.

articles.title: Evolution through large models
AI-written critiques help humans notice flaws
articles.summary: We trained “critique-writing” models to describe flaws in summaries. Human evaluators find flaws in summaries much more often when shown our model’s critiques. Larger models are better at self-critiquing, with scale improving critique-writing more than summary-writing. This shows promise for using AI systems to assist human supervision of AI systems on difficult tasks.

articles.title: Techniques for training large neural networks

articles.title: Image GPT
articles.summary: We find that, just as a large transformer model trained on language can generate coherent text, the same exact model trained on pixel sequences can generate coherent image completions and samples. By establishing a correlation between sample quality and image classification accuracy, we show that our best generative model also contains features competitive with top convolutional nets in the unsupervised setting.

articles.title: Language models are few-shot learners
AI and efficiency
articles.summary: We’re releasing an analysis showing that since 2012 the amount of compute needed to train a neural net to the same performance on ImageNet classification has been decreasing by a factor of 2 every 16 months. Compared to 2012, it now takes 44 times less compute to train a neural network to the level of AlexNet (by contrast, Moore’s Law would yield an 11x cost improvement over this period). Our results suggest that for AI tasks with high levels of recent investment, algorithmic progress has yielded more gains than classical hardware efficiency.

articles.title: Jukebox
articles.summary: We’re introducing Jukebox, a neural net that generates music, including rudimentary singing, as raw audio in a variety of genres and artist styles. We’re releasing the model weights and code, along with a tool to explore the generated samples.

articles.title: Improving verifiability in AI development
articles.summary: We’ve contributed to a multi-stakeholder report by 58 co-authors at 30 organizations, including the Centre for the Future of Intelligence, Mila, Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society, Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences, and Center for Security and Emerging Technologies. This report describes 10 mechanisms to improve the verifiability of claims made about AI systems. Developers can use these tools to provide evidence that AI systems are safe, secure, fair, or privacy-preserving. Users, policymakers, and civil society can use these tools to evaluate AI development processes.

articles.title: OpenAI Microscope
articles.summary: We’re introducing OpenAI Microscope, a collection of visualizations of every significant layer and neuron of eight vision “model organisms” which are often studied in interpretability. Microscope makes it easier to analyze the features that form inside these neural networks, and we hope it will help the research community as we move towards understanding these complicated systems.

articles.title: OpenAI standardizes on PyTorch
articles.summary: We are standardizing OpenAI’s deep learning framework on PyTorch.

articles.title: Scaling laws for neural language models
Dota 2 with large scale deep reinforcement learning
Deep double descent
articles.summary: We show that the double descent phenomenon occurs in CNNs, ResNets, and transformers: performance first improves, then gets worse, and then improves again with increasing model size, data size, or training time. This effect is often avoided through careful regularization. While this behavior appears to be fairly universal, we don’t yet fully understand why it happens, and view further study of this phenomenon as an important research direction.

articles.title: Procgen Benchmark

articles.title: GPT-2: 1.5B release
articles.summary: As the final model release of GPT-2’s staged release, we’re releasing the largest version (1.5B parameters) of GPT-2 along with code and model weights to facilitate detection of outputs of GPT-2 models. While there have been larger language models released since August, we’ve continued with our original staged release plan in order to provide the community with a test case of a full staged release process. We hope that this test case will be useful to developers of future powerful models, and we’re actively continuing the conversation with the AI community on responsible publication.

articles.title: Solving Rubik’s Cube with a robot hand
articles.summary: We’ve trained a pair of neural networks to solve the Rubik’s Cube with a human-like robot hand. The neural networks are trained entirely in simulation, using the same reinforcement learning code as OpenAI Five paired with a new technique called Automatic Domain Randomization (ADR). The system can handle situations it never saw during training, such as being prodded by a stuffed giraffe. This shows that reinforcement learning isn’t just a tool for virtual tasks, but can solve physical-world problems requiring unprecedented dexterity.

articles.title: OpenAI Scholars 2020: Applications open
articles.summary: We are now accepting applications for our third class of OpenAI Scholars.

articles.title: Fine-tuning GPT-2 from human preferences
articles.summary: We’ve fine-tuned the 774M parameter GPT-2 language model using human feedback for various tasks, successfully matching the preferences of the external human labelers, though those preferences did not always match our own. Specifically, for summarization tasks the labelers preferred sentences copied wholesale from the input (we’d only asked them to ensure accuracy), so our models learned to copy. Summarization required 60k human labels; simpler tasks which continue text in various styles required only 5k. Our motivation is to move safety techniques closer to the general task of “machines talking to humans,” which we believe is key to extracting information about human values.

articles.title: Emergent tool use from multi-agent interaction
articles.summary: We’ve observed agents discovering progressively more complex tool use while playing a simple game of hide-and-seek. Through training in our new simulated hide-and-seek environment, agents build a series of six distinct strategies and counterstrategies, some of which we did not know our environment supported. The self-supervised emergent complexity in this simple environment further suggests that multi-agent co-adaptation may one day produce extremely complex and intelligent behavior.

articles.title: Testing robustness against unforeseen adversaries
articles.summary: We’ve developed a method to assess whether a neural network classifier can reliably defend against adversarial attacks not seen during training. Our method yields a new metric, UAR (Unforeseen Attack Robustness), which evaluates the robustness of a single model against an unanticipated attack, and highlights the need to measure performance across a more diverse range of unforeseen attacks.

articles.title: GPT-2: 6-month follow-up
articles.summary: We’re releasing the 774 million parameter GPT-2 language model after the release of our small 124M model in February, staged release of our medium 355M model in May, and subsequent research with partners and the AI community into the model’s potential for misuse and societal benefit. We’re also releasing an open-source legal agreement to make it easier for organizations to initiate model-sharing partnerships with each other, and are publishing a technical report about our experience in coordinating with the wider AI research community on publication norms.

articles.title: Learning Day
articles.summary: At OpenAI, each Thursday is Learning Day: a day where employees have the option to self-study technical skills that will make them better at their job but which aren’t being learned from daily work.

articles.title: Microsoft invests in and partners with OpenAI to support us building beneficial AGI
articles.summary: Microsoft is investing $1 billion in OpenAI to support us building artificial general intelligence (AGI) with widely distributed economic benefits. We’re partnering to develop a hardware and software platform within Microsoft Azure which will scale to AGI. We’ll jointly develop new Azure AI supercomputing technologies, and Microsoft will become our exclusive cloud provider—so we’ll be working hard together to further extend Microsoft Azure’s capabilities in large-scale AI systems.

articles.title: Why responsible AI development needs cooperation on safety
articles.summary: We’ve written a policy research paper identifying four strategies that can be used today to improve the likelihood of long-term industry cooperation on safety norms in AI: communicating risks and benefits, technical collaboration, increased transparency, and incentivizing standards. Our analysis shows that industry cooperation on safety will be instrumental in ensuring that AI systems are safe and beneficial, but competitive pressures could lead to a collective action problem, potentially causing AI companies to under-invest in safety. We hope these strategies will encourage greater cooperation on the safe development of AI and lead to better global outcomes of AI.

articles.title: OpenAI Robotics Symposium 2019
articles.summary: We hosted the first OpenAI Robotics Symposium on April 27, 2019.

articles.title: OpenAI Scholars 2019: Final projects
articles.summary: Our second class of OpenAI Scholars has concluded, with all eight scholars producing an exciting final project showcased at Scholars Demo Day at OpenAI.

articles.title: OpenAI Fellows Fall 2018: Final projects
articles.summary: Our second class of OpenAI Fellows has wrapped up, with each Fellow going from a machine learning beginner to core OpenAI contributor in the course of a 6-month apprenticeship. We are currently reviewing applications on a rolling basis for our next round of OpenAI Fellows Summer 2019.

articles.title: Transfer of adversarial robustness between perturbation types
MuseNet
articles.summary: We’ve created MuseNet, a deep neural network that can generate 4-minute musical compositions with 10 different instruments, and can combine styles from country to Mozart to the Beatles. MuseNet was not explicitly programmed with our understanding of music, but instead discovered patterns of harmony, rhythm, and style by learning to predict the next token in hundreds of thousands of MIDI files. MuseNet uses the same general-purpose unsupervised technology as GPT-2, a large-scale transformer model trained to predict the next token in a sequence, whether audio or text.

articles.title: Generative modeling with sparse transformers
articles.summary: We’ve developed the Sparse Transformer, a deep neural network which sets new records at predicting what comes next in a sequence—whether text, images, or sound. It uses an algorithmic improvement of the attention mechanism to extract patterns from sequences 30x longer than possible previously.

articles.title: OpenAI Five defeats Dota 2 world champions
articles.summary: OpenAI Five is the first AI to beat the world champions in an esports game, having won two back-to-back games versus the world champion Dota 2 team, OG, at Finals this weekend. Both OpenAI Five and DeepMind’s AlphaStar had previously beaten good pros privately but lost their live pro matches, making this also the first time an AI has beaten esports pros on livestream.

articles.title: OpenAI Five Finals
articles.summary: We’ll be holding our final live event for OpenAI Five at 11:30am PT on April 13.

articles.title: Implicit generation and generalization methods for energy-based models
articles.summary: We’ve made progress towards stable and scalable training of energy-based models (EBMs) resulting in better sample quality and generalization ability than existing models. Generation in EBMs spends more compute to continually refine its answers and doing so can generate samples competitive with GANs at low temperatures, while also having mode coverage guarantees of likelihood-based models. We hope these findings stimulate further research into this promising class of models.

articles.title: OpenAI Scholars 2019: Meet our Scholars
articles.summary: Our class of eight scholars (out of 550 applicants) brings together collective expertise in literature, philosophy, cell biology, statistics, economics, quantum physics, and business innovation.

articles.title: OpenAI LP
articles.summary: We’ve created OpenAI LP, a new “capped-profit” company that allows us to rapidly increase our investments in compute and talent while including checks and balances to actualize our mission.

articles.title: Introducing Activation Atlases
articles.summary: We’ve created activation atlases (in collaboration with Google researchers), a new technique for visualizing what interactions between neurons can represent. As AI systems are deployed in increasingly sensitive contexts, having a better understanding of their internal decision-making processes will let us identify weaknesses and investigate failures.

articles.title: Neural MMO: A massively multiagent game environment
articles.summary: We’re releasing a Neural MMO, a massively multiagent game environment for reinforcement learning agents. Our platform supports a large, variable number of agents within a persistent and open-ended task. The inclusion of many agents and species leads to better exploration, divergent niche formation, and greater overall competence.

articles.title: Spinning Up in Deep RL: Workshop review
articles.summary: On February 2, we held our first Spinning Up Workshop as part of our new education initiative at OpenAI.

articles.title: AI safety needs social scientists
articles.summary: We’ve written a paper arguing that long-term AI safety research needs social scientists to ensure AI alignment algorithms succeed when actual humans are involved. Properly aligning advanced AI systems with human values requires resolving many uncertainties related to the psychology of human rationality, emotion, and biases. The aim of this paper is to spark further collaboration between machine learning and social science researchers, and we plan to hire social scientists to work on this full time at OpenAI.

articles.title: Better language models and their implications
articles.summary: We’ve trained a large-scale unsupervised language model which generates coherent paragraphs of text, achieves state-of-the-art performance on many language modeling benchmarks, and performs rudimentary reading comprehension, machine translation, question answering, and summarization—all without task-specific training.

articles.title: Computational limitations in robust classification and win-win results
OpenAI Fellows Summer 2018: Final projects
articles.summary: Our first cohort of OpenAI Fellows has concluded, with each Fellow going from a machine learning beginner to core OpenAI contributor in the course of a 6-month apprenticeship.

articles.title: How AI training scales
articles.summary: We’ve discovered that the gradient noise scale, a simple statistical metric, predicts the parallelizability of neural network training on a wide range of tasks. Since complex tasks tend to have noisier gradients, increasingly large batch sizes are likely to become useful in the future, removing one potential limit to further growth of AI systems. More broadly, these results show that neural network training need not be considered a mysterious art, but can be rigorized and systematized.

articles.title: Quantifying generalization in reinforcement learning
articles.summary: We’re releasing CoinRun, a training environment which provides a metric for an agent’s ability to transfer its experience to novel situations and has already helped clarify a longstanding puzzle in reinforcement learning. CoinRun strikes a desirable balance in complexity: the environment is simpler than traditional platformer games like Sonic the Hedgehog but still poses a worthy generalization challenge for state of the art algorithms.

articles.title: Spinning Up in Deep RL
articles.summary: We’re releasing Spinning Up in Deep RL, an educational resource designed to let anyone learn to become a skilled practitioner in deep reinforcement learning. Spinning Up consists of crystal-clear examples of RL code, educational exercises, documentation, and tutorials.

articles.title: Learning concepts with energy functions
articles.summary: We’ve developed an energy-based model that can quickly learn to identify and generate instances of concepts, such as near, above, between, closest, and furthest, expressed as sets of 2d points. Our model learns these concepts after only five demonstrations. We also show cross-domain transfer: we use concepts learned in a 2d particle environment to solve tasks on a 3-dimensional physics-based robot.

articles.title: Plan online, learn offline: Efficient learning and exploration via model-based control
Reinforcement learning with prediction-based rewards
articles.summary: We’ve developed Random Network Distillation (RND), a prediction-based method for encouraging reinforcement learning agents to explore their environments through curiosity, which for the first time exceeds average human performance on Montezuma’s Revenge.

articles.title: Learning complex goals with iterated amplification
articles.summary: We’re proposing an AI safety technique called iterated amplification that lets us specify complicated behaviors and goals that are beyond human scale, by demonstrating how to decompose a task into simpler sub-tasks, rather than by providing labeled data or a reward function. Although this idea is in its very early stages and we have only completed experiments on simple toy algorithmic domains, we’ve decided to present it in its preliminary state because we think it could prove to be a scalable approach to AI safety.

articles.title: Glow: Better reversible generative models
articles.summary: We introduce Glow, a reversible generative model which uses invertible 1x1 convolutions. It extends previous work on reversible generative models and simplifies the architecture. Our model can generate realistic high resolution images, supports efficient sampling, and discovers features that can be used to manipulate attributes of data. We’re releasing code for the model and an online visualization tool so people can explore and build on these results.

articles.title: Learning Montezuma’s Revenge from a single demonstration
articles.summary: We’ve trained an agent to achieve a high score of 74,500 on Montezuma’s Revenge from a single human demonstration, better than any previously published result. Our algorithm is simple: the agent plays a sequence of games starting from carefully chosen states from the demonstration, and learns from them by optimizing the game score using PPO, the same reinforcement learning algorithm that underpins OpenAI Five.

articles.title: OpenAI Five
articles.summary: Our team of five neural networks, OpenAI Five, has started to defeat amateur human teams at Dota 2.

articles.title: Retro Contest: Results

articles.title: Learning policy representations in multiagent systems
Improving language understanding with unsupervised learning
articles.summary: We’ve obtained state-of-the-art results on a suite of diverse language tasks with a scalable, task-agnostic system, which we’re also releasing. Our approach is a combination of two existing ideas: transformers and unsupervised pre-training. These results provide a convincing example that pairing supervised learning methods with unsupervised pre-training works very well; this is an idea that many have explored in the past, and we hope our result motivates further research into applying this idea on larger and more diverse datasets.

articles.title: Gym Retro
articles.summary: We’re releasing the full version of Gym Retro, a platform for reinforcement learning research on games. This brings our publicly-released game count from around 70 Atari games and 30 Sega games to over 1,000 games across a variety of backing emulators. We’re also releasing the tool we use to add new games to the platform.

articles.title: AI and compute
articles.summary: We’re releasing an analysis showing that since 2012, the amount of compute used in the largest AI training runs has been increasing exponentially with a 3.4-month doubling time (by comparison, Moore’s Law had a 2-year doubling period)[^footnote-correction]. Since 2012, this metric has grown by more than 300,000x (a 2-year doubling period would yield only a 7x increase). Improvements in compute have been a key component of AI progress, so as long as this trend continues, it’s worth preparing for the implications of systems far outside today’s capabilities.

articles.title: AI safety via debate
articles.summary: We’re proposing an AI safety technique which trains agents to debate topics with one another, using a human to judge who wins.

articles.title: Evolved Policy Gradients
articles.summary: We’re releasing an experimental metalearning approach called Evolved Policy Gradients, a method that evolves the loss function of learning agents, which can enable fast training on novel tasks. Agents trained with EPG can succeed at basic tasks at test time that were outside their training regime, like learning to navigate to an object on a different side of the room from where it was placed during training.

On first-order meta-learning algorithms
Reptile: A scalable meta-learning algorithm
articles.summary: We’ve developed a simple meta-learning algorithm called Reptile which works by repeatedly sampling a task, performing stochastic gradient descent on it, and updating the initial parameters towards the final parameters learned on that task. Reptile is the application of the Shortest Descent algorithm to the meta-learning setting, and is mathematically similar to first-order MAML (which is a version of the well-known MAML algorithm) that only needs black-box access to an optimizer such as SGD or Adam, with similar computational efficiency and performance.

Ingredients for robotics research

We’ve used these environments to train models which work on physical robots. We’re also releasing a set of requests for robotics research.

articles.title: Preparing for malicious uses of AI
articles.summary: We’ve co-authored a paper that forecasts how malicious actors could misuse AI technology, and potential ways we can prevent and mitigate these threats. This paper is the outcome of almost a year of sustained work with our colleagues at the Future of Humanity Institute, the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk, the Center for a New American Security, the Electronic Frontier Foundation, and others.

articles.title: OpenAI supporters
articles.summary: We’re excited to welcome new donors to OpenAI.

articles.title: Interpretable machine learning through teaching
articles.summary: We’ve designed a method that encourages AIs to teach each other with examples that also make sense to humans. Our approach automatically selects the most informative examples to teach a concept—for instance, the best images to describe the concept of dogs—and experimentally we found our approach to be effective at teaching both AIs

articles.title: Discovering types for entity disambiguation
articles.summary: We’ve built a system for automatically figuring out which object is meant by a word by having a neural network decide if the word belongs to each of about 100 automatically-discovered “types” (non-exclusive categories).

articles.title: Scaling Kubernetes to 2,500 nodes
Block-sparse GPU kernels
articles.summary: We’re releasing highly-optimized GPU kernels for an underexplored class of neural network architectures: networks with block-sparse weights. Depending on the chosen sparsity, these kernels can run orders of magnitude faster than cuBLAS or cuSPARSE. We’ve used them to attain state-of-the-art results in text sentiment analysis and generative modeling of text and images.

articles.title: Learning sparse neural networks through L₀ regularization
Interpretable and pedagogical examples
Learning a hierarchy
articles.summary: We’ve developed a hierarchical reinforcement learning algorithm that learns high-level actions useful for solving a range of tasks, allowing fast solving of tasks requiring thousands of timesteps. Our algorithm, when applied to a set of navigation problems, discovers a set of high-level actions for walking and crawling in different directions, which enables the agent to master new navigation tasks quickly.

articles.title: Generalizing from simulation
articles.summary: Our latest robotics techniques allow robot controllers, trained entirely in simulation and deployed on physical robots, to react to unplanned changes in the environment as they solve simple tasks. That is, we’ve used these techniques to build closed-loop systems rather than open-loop ones as before.

articles.title: Asymmetric actor critic for image-based robot learning
Sim-to-real transfer of robotic control with dynamics randomization
Domain randomization and generative models for robotic grasping
Competitive self-play
articles.summary: We’ve found that self-play allows simulated AIs to discover physical skills like tackling, ducking, faking, kicking, catching, and diving for the ball, without explicitly designing an environment with these skills in mind. Self-play ensures that the environment is always the right difficulty for an AI to improve. Taken alongside our Dota 2 self-play results, we have increasing confidence that self-play will be a core part of powerful AI systems in the future.

articles.title: Meta-learning for wrestling
articles.summary: We show that for the task of simulated robot wrestling, a meta-learning agent can learn to quickly defeat a stronger non-meta-learning agent, and also show that the meta-learning agent can adapt to physical malfunction.

articles.title: Nonlinear computation in deep linear networks
Learning to model other minds
articles.summary: We’re releasing an algorithm which accounts for the fact that other agents are learning too, and discovers self-interested yet collaborative strategies like tit-for-tat in the iterated prisoner’s dilemma. This algorithm, Learning with Opponent-Learning Awareness (LOLA), is a small step towards agents that model other minds.

articles.title: Learning with opponent-learning awareness
OpenAI Baselines: ACKTR & A2C
articles.summary: We’re releasing two new OpenAI Baselines implementations: ACKTR and A2C. A2C is a synchronous, deterministic variant of Asynchronous Advantage Actor Critic (A3C) which we’ve found gives equal performance. ACKTR is a more sample-efficient reinforcement learning algorithm than TRPO and A2C, and requires only slightly more computation than A2C per update.

articles.title: More on Dota 2
articles.summary: Our Dota 2 result shows that self-play can catapult the performance of machine learning systems from far below human level to superhuman, given sufficient compute. In the span of a month, our system went from barely matching a high-ranked player to beating the top pros and has continued to improve since then. Supervised deep learning systems can only be as good as their training datasets, but in self-play systems, the available data improves automatically as the agent gets better.

articles.title: Dota 2
articles.summary: We’ve created a bot which beats the world’s top professionals at 1v1 matches of Dota 2 under standard tournament rules. The bot learned the game from scratch by self-play, and does not use imitation learning or tree search. This is a step towards building AI systems which accomplish well-defined goals in messy, complicated situations involving real humans.

articles.title: Gathering human feedback
articles.summary: RL-Teacher is an open-source implementation of our interface to train AIs via occasional human feedback rather than hand-crafted reward functions. The underlying technique was developed as a step towards safe AI systems, but also applies to reinforcement learning problems with rewards that are hard to specify.

articles.title: Better exploration with parameter noise
articles.summary: We’ve found that adding adaptive noise to the parameters of reinforcement learning algorithms frequently boosts performance. This exploration method is simple to implement and very rarely decreases performance, so it’s worth trying on any problem.

articles.title: Proximal Policy Optimization
articles.summary: We’re releasing a new class of reinforcement learning algorithms, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which perform comparably or better than state-of-the-art approaches while being much simpler to implement and tune. PPO has become the default reinforcement learning algorithm at OpenAI because of its ease of use and good performance.

articles.title: Robust adversarial inputs
articles.summary: We’ve created images that reliably fool neural network classifiers when viewed from varied scales and perspectives. This challenges a claim from last week that self-driving cars would be hard to trick maliciously since they capture images from multiple scales, angles, perspectives, and the like.

articles.title: Learning from human preferences
articles.summary: One step towards building safe AI systems is to remove the need for humans to write goal functions, since using a simple proxy for a complex goal, or getting the complex goal a bit wrong, can lead to undesirable and even dangerous behavior. In collaboration with DeepMind’s safety team, we’ve developed an algorithm which can infer what humans want by being told which of two proposed behaviors is better.

articles.title: Learning to cooperate, compete, and communicate
articles.summary: Multiagent environments where agents compete for resources are stepping stones on the path to AGI. Multiagent environments have two useful properties: first, there is a natural curriculum—the difficulty of the environment is determined by the skill of your competitors (and if you’re competing against clones of yourself, the environment exactly matches your skill level). Second, a multiagent environment has no stable equilibrium: no matter how smart an agent is, there’s always pressure to get smarter. These environments have a very different feel from traditional environments, and it’ll take a lot more research before we become good at them.

articles.title: Robots that learn

articles.summary: Adversarial examples are inputs to machine learning models that an attacker has intentionally designed to cause the model to make a mistake; they’re like optical illusions for machines. In this post we’ll show how adversarial examples work across different mediums, and will discuss why securing systems against them can be difficult.

articles.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
articles.summary: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights: We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin , then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up. Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one: I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4. It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look. I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark. articles.title: Ladybird's first alpha release
articles.summary:
Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS . This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha , which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself! I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool): Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script , thanks Claude): Ladybird (72925)  [240 MB]
└── Hub (72926)  [61 MB]
    ├── RequestServer (72927)  [29 MB]
    ├── ProcessReaper (72928)  [1 MB]
    ├── Compositor (72930)  [123 MB]
    ├── RequestServer (72953)  [36 MB]
    ├── WebContent (72984)  [819 MB]
    ├── MediaServer (73006)  [118 MB]
    ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007)  [20 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73052)  [144 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73057)  [73 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73073)  [166 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73094)  [70 MB]
    ├── WebContent (73112)  [116 MB]
    ├── RequestServer (73113)  [27 MB]
    └── WebContent (73185)  [60 MB] Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site). I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool . It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too. The one thing I tried that didn't work was Datasette Lite , which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error: undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages') I filed an issue about this , then found a FIXME annotation in the source code. The October explosion The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI , describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex. Here's the GitHub contributions chart for Ladybird over the past twelve months: That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements. This Month in Ladybird — October 2026 describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the JetStream 3 WASM benchmark , they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest web-platform-tests suite, beating Safari! How did they do that? Coding agents: Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing . I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October. Should you use Ladybird? Here's what Andreas says about Ladybird's suitability for use as a daily browser: This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details. We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird! Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won't be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts. I'm going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings. Tags: browsers , open-source , ai , rust , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , andreas-kling , ladybird , coding-agents

articles.title: Muru
articles.summary: Muru Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since. Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production. As he did with wrapture , he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process. Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks: 2026-11-04 — Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next 2026-11-05 — A first look at Muru 2026-11-07 — Muru: looking inside the workers 2026-11-08 — Muru: how it fits together 2026-11-09 — Muru: import once, fork many 2026-11-10 — Muru: HTTPS in development 2026-11-11 — Muru: WSGI and ASGI together 2026-11-11 — AI as a lifestyle choice 2026-11-12 — Muru: releases, not restarts 2026-11-13 — Muru: canaries without a service mesh 2026-11-14 — Muru: a better tenant in a container 2026-11-15 — Muru: working with Kubernetes, not around it 2026-11-16 — Muru: scaling from what the workers report 2026-11-17 — Muru: scaling to zero 2026-11-18 — Muru: overlays on a schedule 2026-11-19 — Muru: noticing and responding 2026-11-20 — Muru: a toolbar on every page 2026-11-21 — Muru: tracing in the toolbar 2026-11-22 — Muru: when lazy imports help That post about AI as a lifestyle choice is particularly worth a read: The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too. articles.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
articles.summary: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube) Claire Vo runs ChatPRD , an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post ) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse. Tags: youtube , ai , generative-ai , llms , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , ai-misuse

articles.summary: Release: llm-gemini 0.38 Today Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon . I wrote recently about how confusing the pricing for the Gemini 4 series was - Neon has somehow made this even worse. Previously the Gemini 4 lineup was Hydrogen, Argon, and Carbon - where Argon and Carbon were the same price , and Hydrogen was 3/4 of that price now but will be 1/4 of that price when the other two double an 1st December once their initial discount pricing expires. The Neon announcement pretends that Argon doesn't exist. Here's their new image explaining the model line-up: So the lineup now, from most to least expensive, is Carbon, Neon, Hydrogen. Except Carbon is currently half price, so right now Neon ($3/million input, $15/million output) is the most expensive of the three - then Carbon ($2/$10), then Hydrogen ($1.50/$7.50). I guess this will make more sense when Carbon doubles to $4/$20 on December 1st. I ran some pelicans through the three reasoning levels for Neon - low, medium, high. articles.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
articles.summary: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. Tags: sandboxing , security , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , claude-code , codex , pi
